To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

benthic nitrogen fixation in sediments of Peruvian OMZ was detected at all stations, and the activity distribution of nitrogen fixation was positively correlated to the organic matter content and negatively to free sulfide concentration.
N2 fixation rates were in the same order of magnitude in OMZ sediments as in other anoxic sediments and that N2 fixation and sulfur cycling were coupled.
benthic nitrogen fixation in sediments of an oxygen minimum zone was controlled by organic matter and free sulfide and that the nifH gene pool was diverse, with a weak link to sulfate reducers.

the potential coupling of N2 fixation and anaerobic respiration in the OMZ sediments of the Eastern Tropical South Pacific.

N2 fixation in Peruvian OMZ sediment was not coupled to SR but was controlled by the supply of organic matter and free sulfide.
the potential coupling of N2 fixation and SO4 2− reduction is not a common feature in the Peruvian sediments, but that it is possible under certain conditions.
N2 fixation and SO4−2 reduction are not coupled in the Peruvian oxygen-minimum zone, but that N2 fixation is controlled by organic carbon supply and sulfide concentrations.

The main takeaway from our work is that

benthic nitrogen fixation is not restricted to oxygenated bottom waters, but can occur in anoxic and hypoxia sediments as well, and that it is controlled by different environmental factors than in the water column.
benthic nitrogen fixation in the Peru OMZ is not coupled to the OMZ, and that the OMZ does not represent a hotspot of nitrogen fixation.
N2 fixation in sediments of OMZs can contribute to N2 supply to the water column and the overlying ocean.
